title: Self-Paced Module: The Four Pillars of OOP in Java

objectives.cognitive: Explain private fields, getters and a validating setter.
objectives.affective: Respect rules that protect another object's data.
objectives.psychomotor: Run a complete Vehicle class and change a setter argument.

blocks.markdown: This JSON follows the printed three-session catch-up sequence. Day 2 contains three successive pillars; the five-day lesson plan supplies the teaching objectives. Work through each part in order. Each sample is followed by a small alteration with its own expected output. Paper liplets are submitted to the teacher and never block online progress.
Encapsulation protects data; inheritance reuses a parent; polymorphism lets one call take different forms; abstraction shows a contract while leaving details to children.
Bundle data and methods in one class. Make fields private and use public methods to read or change them. A setter can reject an invalid value.
An ATM protects its money. You ask through its controls instead of touching the cash. A validating setter is that controlled door.

lessons.title: Abstraction: require each child to implement the contract

objectives.cognitive: Explain abstract classes and abstract methods.
objectives.affective: Value clear responsibilities over hidden assumptions.
objectives.psychomotor: Run an abstract Vehicle family with all required overrides.

blocks.markdown: An abstract class describes a shared idea and cannot be instantiated directly. An abstract method has no body; each concrete child must implement it.

performanceTask.title: Build and present your own OOP program
performanceTask.markdown: Use the Vehicle program as your model, then build a different theme: sari-sari store items, school personnel/pay, pets/care cost, gadgets/warranty, shapes/area, or a teacher-approved theme. Do not copy the Vehicle theme. Work in the separate personal project. Plan class names, fields, methods and setter validation before coding. Run and save as often as needed; submit explicitly when ready. Paper liplets and teacher assessment remain separate.
steps: Choose your theme: sari-sari store items, school personnel and pay, pets and care cost, gadgets and warranty, shapes and area, or one your teacher approves. Not vehicles.
On paper, plan your parent class, at least two child classes, their private fields, one abstract method, and one setter rule that refuses bad data. Show your teacher.
In Projects, click **Personal performance-task project**. Add a file for your parent class.

Open **Code from this module** and click **Copy code** on **Step 1 · Vehicle.java**. Paste it into your parent file, then rename the class, fields, constructor and getters for your theme. Keep `this.` in the constructor.
Change the setter so it refuses bad data for your theme, like `setPassengers` refuses -3. **Run code** and check that a bad value is refused.
Add a file for each child. Copy **Step 3 · Jeepney.java**, paste it, and change it: `extends` your parent, call `super(...)`, and add one private field with its getter.
Make your parent `abstract` with one abstract method, like `computeFare` in **Step 8 · Vehicle.java**. Each child overrides it in its own way.
In `Main.java`, make a parent-type array that holds objects of each child, and loop over it calling the overridden method, like **Step 6 · Main.java**. **Run code**.
Add a comment naming each pillar where it appears: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction.
Tick each item in the **Performance task checklist**, then click **Submit this version**.
checklist: One abstract parent with at least one abstract method
At least three private parent fields, constructor using this, and getters
At least one validating setter that refuses bad data
At least two children using extends and super(...)
Each child adds a private field and getter
Each child overrides the abstract method differently
Main uses a parent-type array and loop
Use a different theme and Submit this version explicitly
